authoring_notes: Domain 6 quality pass: every node now combines short ADHD-friendly progressive explanations with its existing code example. Each code example has one click-to-reveal result panel. Progressive text hides one key phrase normally and at most two. Glossary terms are scoped per node and explain supporting vocabulary only. reveal.text: `itertools.chain()` creates a lazy iterator that yields each iterable in sequence.

reveal.code:
from itertools import chain

first = [1, 2]
second = [3, 4]
combined = list(chain(first, second))

annotations.title: Lazy concatenation
annotations.explanation: chain yields all items from first, then all items from second.

prompts.label: INPUTS ARE CONSUMED LEFT TO RIGHT

reveal.text: The iterator exhausts the first iterable before moving to the next iterable.

prompts.label: USE FROM_ITERABLE FOR AN ITERABLE OF GROUPS

reveal.text: `chain.from_iterable(groups)` flattens one level when the groups themselves arrive through an iterable.

reveal.text: `itertools.batched()` is Python 3.12+ and creates a lazy iterator that groups input into tuple batches.

reveal.code:
from itertools import batched

values = range(10)
chunks = list(batched(values, 3))

annotations.title: Fixed-size batches
annotations.explanation: Successive tuples contain up to three items; the final batch may be shorter.

prompts.label: THE FINAL BATCH MAY BE SHORTER

reveal.text: Without strict mode, the final tuple can contain fewer than `n` items.
`batched(..., strict=True)` is Python 3.13+ and raises `ValueError` for an incomplete final batch.

reveal.text: `pairwise()` returns an iterator of adjacent pairs such as `(a, b)`, then `(b, c)`.
With fewer than two input values, `pairwise()` produces no pairs.

reveal.text: `itertools.pairwise()` was added in Python 3.10, the oldest version covered by this track.

reveal.text: `starmap(func, rows)` lazily expands each argument tuple into positional arguments for `func`.

reveal.code:
from itertools import starmap
from operator import mul

pairs = [(2, 3), (4, 5), (6, 7)]
products = list(starmap(mul, pairs))

annotations.title: Map argument tuples
annotations.explanation: starmap calls mul(2,3), mul(4,5), and mul(6,7).

prompts.label: MAP AND STARMAP EXPECT DIFFERENT ITEM SHAPES

reveal.text: Use `map()` when each input item is one argument; use `starmap()` when each item should be unpacked.
Like other itertools tools, `starmap()` is lazy and does not build the complete result list by itself.

reveal.text: `Path` overloads `/` so each path segment can be joined without manually writing platform separators.

reveal.code:
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("data")
config = root / "settings" / "app.json"
text = config.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

annotations.title: Compose path segments
annotations.explanation: Path overloads / so you do not manually concatenate separators.

annotations.title: Read text through Path
annotations.explanation: Path provides direct filesystem convenience methods.

prompts.label: A PATH OBJECT DOES NOT CREATE THE FILE

reveal.text: Constructing a `Path` describes a filesystem location; it does not guarantee that the target exists.
`read_text(encoding='utf-8')` decodes file bytes with the requested encoding and closes the file afterward.

glossary.definition: One component of a filesystem path, such as a directory name or filename.
The operating system's organization of files and directories.
The mapping used to convert between text characters and bytes, such as UTF-8.

reveal.text: `subprocess.run()` waits for the child process and returns a `CompletedProcess` containing its exit status.

prompts.label: RUN A COMMAND WITHOUT SHELL PARSING
prompts.placeholder: Click the argument list, check, and capture_output.

reveal.code:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ["git", "status", "--short"],
    check=True,
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)

print(result.stdout)

annotations.title: Argument vector
annotations.explanation: Program and arguments stay separate instead of being parsed from one shell string.

annotations.title: Capture stdout/stderr
annotations.explanation: The completed-process object receives captured streams.

annotations.title: Decode as text
annotations.explanation: stdout/stderr are strings instead of bytes.

prompts.label: CHECK, CAPTURE, AND TEXT CONTROL DIFFERENT THINGS

reveal.text: `check=True` raises on failure; `capture_output=True` captures stdout and stderr; `text=True` returns strings.

prompts.label: PREFER ARGUMENT LISTS FOR ORDINARY COMMANDS

reveal.text: Avoid `shell=True` with untrusted text because shell parsing can create shell injection vulnerabilities.

glossary.definition: The integer code a process returns when it finishes; zero usually means success.
The standard output stream where a process normally writes ordinary output.
A security flaw where untrusted text changes the meaning of a command interpreted by a shell.

reveal.text: `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` creates an aware UTC datetime whose `tzinfo` is explicit.

reveal.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

now_utc = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
tokyo = now_utc.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))

annotations.title: Aware UTC datetime
annotations.explanation: The datetime carries explicit timezone information.

annotations.title: Convert the same instant
annotations.explanation: astimezone applies the target zone's offset rules.

result.output: tokyo represents the same instant as now_utc with Asia/Tokyo's offset rules

prompts.label: ASTIMEZONE CHANGES REPRESENTATION, NOT THE INSTANT

reveal.text: `astimezone()` represents the same instant using the target IANA time zone rules.
`datetime.utcnow()` has `tzinfo=None` and is deprecated since Python 3.12; prefer an aware UTC datetime.

reveal.text: `json.dumps(..., default=func)` calls the serializer only for values the normal encoder cannot make JSON-encodable.

reveal.code:
import json
from datetime import datetime

payload = {"created_at": datetime(2026, 9, 19, 12, 0)}

text = json.dumps(
    payload,
    default=lambda value: value.isoformat(),
)

annotations.title: Fallback serializer
annotations.explanation: The hook converts unsupported objects into JSON-encodable values.

prompts.label: THE HOOK MUST RETURN A SUPPORTED VALUE

reveal.text: The default hook should return a JSON-supported value or raise `TypeError` for an unsupported object.
`default=str` is convenient but can silently turn accidental unsupported objects into strings instead of exposing a modeling error.

reveal.text: `heapq.nlargest(n, items, key=...)` returns the top-k original items according to the key function.

reveal.code:
from heapq import nlargest

records = [
    {"name": "a", "score": 7},
    {"name": "b", "score": 10},
    {"name": "c", "score": 9},
]

top_two = nlargest(2, records, key=lambda row: row["score"])

annotations.title: Top-k selection
annotations.explanation: nlargest returns the two largest records according to the key.

annotations.title: Comparison key
annotations.explanation: Records are compared by score while original records are returned.

prompts.label: IT IS BEST WHEN N IS SMALL

reveal.text: `nlargest()` performs best for smaller `n`; a full sort can be better when `n` is large.

prompts.label: USE MAX() FOR A SINGLE LARGEST ITEM

reveal.text: When `n == 1`, the built-in `max()` is more efficient than `nlargest(1, ...)`.

glossary.definition: The k highest-ranked items from a larger collection.
A function passed with `key=` that computes the comparison value for each item.
Ordering the entire input collection rather than selecting only a small number of extreme values.

reveal.text: `bisect.insort()` uses binary search to find an insertion point that preserves the sorted invariant.

reveal.code:
from bisect import insort

values = [1, 4, 8, 12]
insort(values, 6)

annotations.title: Sorted insertion
annotations.explanation: 6 is inserted at the position that keeps values sorted.

prompts.label: SEARCH IS FAST, INSERTION STILL SHIFTS ITEMS

reveal.text: Finding the position is logarithmic, but list insertion is O(n) because later elements must move.
Concurrent use on the same sequence can break the sorted invariant unless your code provides synchronization.

glossary.definition: The index where a value can be inserted while preserving sorted order.
A search strategy that repeatedly halves the remaining ordered search range.
Linear growth: the amount of work grows roughly with the number of elements.
The requirement that a sequence remain sorted before and after an operation.
